uncited: This family encompasses the fundamental mathematical definitions, spatial transformations, and sampling mechanisms required to define and query scalar distance fields for ray marching.
It solves the problem of representing complex 3D geometry and procedural surfaces as continuous scalar functions $f(\mathbf{p})$, where the zero-level set $f(\mathbf{p}) = 0$ defines the surface.

What sets this family apart from its siblings is its focus on the **definition and retrieval** of the distance value itself, distinct from [Terrain Raymarching](1357-terrain-raymarching.md) which handles height-field specific optimizations, [Neon Raymarcher](4157-neon-raymarcher.md) which focuses on volumetric lighting integration, [Menger Sponge Raymarching](4875-menger-sponge-raymarching.md) which implements specific fractal recursion, and [Fractals and Mathematical Surfaces](10024-fractals-and-mathematical-surfaces.md) which deals with iterative complex number mappings.
The family operates on the principle that a scene is defined by a scalar field $f(\mathbf{p})$ where the zero-level set $f(\mathbf{p}) = 0$ represents the surface.
For sphere tracing to be valid, the function must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring $|f(\mathbf{p}_1) - f(\mathbf{p}_2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}_1 - \mathbf{p}_2\|$.

This guarantees that the value $f(\mathbf{p})$ is a safe lower bound on the distance to the surface, allowing the ray marcher to step forward by exactly $f(\mathbf{p})$ without tunneling [S2, S5, 9643].
Transformations are applied by mapping the query point $\mathbf{p}$ into the local coordinate space of the primitive using the inverse transformation matrix $M^{-1}$ before evaluation [S3850].
Procedural noise (e.g., FBM) is often used to perturb these analytical surfaces, creating hypertextures where the isosurface is defined by $SDF(\mathbf{p}) + B_n(\mathbf{p}) = 0$ [S1].

The concept of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) in computer graphics was popularized by Greg Turk's "Blobby Volumes" (1989) and later formalized for ray marching by Inigo Quilez in his online articles (2009-2010) [S1, S2, S5, 9643].

The Lipschitz continuity requirement for sphere tracing was rigorously established in the context of ray marching by Matt Pharr and Greg Humphreys in "Physically Based Rendering" (2010) and further detailed by Quilez [S2, S5, 9643].

The use of Boolean operations (min/max) for constructive solid geometry (CSG) with SDFs is a standard technique in procedural modeling, attributed to various contributors in the demoscene and real-time rendering communities [S39, unofficial].
